page.title: Choosing a virtual event provider: key decisions
page.description: Learn the first decisions to make when selecting a virtual event provider, from roles and run of show to cost models and risk mitigation.
page.h1: What should you decide first about virtual event providers?
page.definition: A virtual event provider is a company that supplies the platform, production crew, and operational support needed to deliver live online or hybrid experiences. It handles streaming infrastructure, speaker rehearsal, run of show creation, backup streams, and post‑event recording delivery.
page.quick_answer: Define the owner for each production role, lock the platform and rehearsal dates six to eight weeks out, and choose a cost model that matches your attendee capacity before signing any contract.

sections.h2: What roles and responsibilities should be defined before hiring a virtual event provider?

blocks.p: Assign a single owner for each of the eight workstreams so nothing falls through the cracks. The workstreams cover event strategy, platform selection, speaker management, run of show, technical production, moderation, recording and clipping, and reporting.

sections.h2: How do you build a run of show and rehearsal schedule?

blocks.p: Create a detailed run of show and schedule one full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before the event. The rehearsal validates speaker timing, slide cues, and the backup stream.

ol: Draft the run of show with time codes and cue points
Share the draft with all speakers and the production crew
Conduct a technical check sixty minutes before going live
Run the full rehearsal on the actual platform
Capture a parallel backup stream during rehearsal
Deliver the edited replay within twenty four to forty eight hours

sections.h2: Which cost model fits your event size and budget?

blocks.p: Match the pricing structure to your attendee capacity and contract preference. Three cost models exist: per‑host licences sized by attendee capacity, self‑serve monthly plans, and annual contracts quoted by sales.

sections.h2: What are the common single points of failure and how to mitigate them?

blocks.p: Identify the platform, encoder, and speaker connection as the three main failure points and prepare a backup for each. A single point of failure can derail the entire broadcast.

ul: Platform outage – keep a secondary streaming account ready
Encoder crash – run a parallel encoder on a separate machine
Speaker internet loss – require a wired connection and a dial‑in backup

sections.h2: Which tools and platforms integrate with a virtual event provider?

blocks.p: Select a registration, project management, and analytics stack that connects to your chosen event platform. Integration reduces manual hand‑offs and keeps data consistent.

ul: Streaming – Zoom Events, Cvent, or Bizzabo

faq.q: How far in advance should I book a virtual event provider for a summit?
faq.a: Plan a hybrid conference six to eight weeks out; lock the venue AV and the platform before the agenda is final. This lead time lets you confirm speaker slots, run a full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before, and deliver the replay within twenty four to forty eight hours.

faq.q: What is the typical price range for a produced webinar?
faq.a: Moderated webinars cost $2,500 to $7,500 per production according to a published range, directional not a fixed quote. The fee covers a live producer, Q&A moderation, branded slide template, lower thirds, backup stream, and edited recording with clips for attendees.

faq.q: Do I need a separate production crew if I use a self‑serve platform?
faq.a: The platform is not the production; someone still has to own the run of show, rehearse speakers and keep a backup stream ready, even on self‑serve tools. A single producer can run a simple webinar, while summits and hybrid events need a show caller, speaker manager, moderator and platform operator.
